+**No, pick "None/other".** Actual Budget doesn't use create-react-app. The frontend (`desktop-client`) is built with **Vite**, and every package runs its tests with **Vitest**. The CRA preset sets Stryker up to use Jest through `react-scripts`, and this repo has neither, so that config would fail as soon as you ran it.
+
+For the next prompts:
+
+- **Test runner:** choose **vitest**. That installs `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner`.
+- **Reporters:** pick whatever you like. `html` and `clear-text` are the usual choices.
+- **Package manager:** choose **yarn**. Note that Stryker's init installs packages with plain yarn commands, and Yarn 4 workspaces can be picky about that. If the install step fails, add the packages yourself from the repo root, in the workspace you're testing:
+  ```bash
+  yarn workspace @actual-app/core add -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner
+  ```
+
+This repo is a monorepo, so point Stryker at one package rather than the whole repo. `packages/loot-core` is a good place to start because it holds most of the business logic and unit tests. Put the Stryker config in that package and limit the files it mutates with the `mutate` setting, for example `src/server/budget/**/*.ts`. Mutation testing all of loot-core in one run would take a very long time.

+import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'vitest/config';
+
+import baseConfig from './vitest.config';
+
+// Stryker always runs Vitest in the `threads` pool. On Windows the full
+// loot-core suite crashes there (native SQLite in worker threads), so only run
+// the tests for the code Stryker mutates (see `mutate` in stryker.config.json).
+export default mergeConfig(
+  baseConfig,
+  defineConfig({
+    test: {
+      include: ['src/server/budget/**/*.test.ts'],
+    },
+  }),
+);

## PR 91: "[AI] Add StrykerJS mutation testing setup"

This is Bennett's PR (`feat/add-strykerjs` → `master`). It adds Stryker mutation testing to **loot-core** only, and only for `src/server/budget/`. Besides `yarn.lock`, it changes five files:

| File                                          | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json`      | The main config. It uses the Vitest runner, mutates `src/server/budget/**/*.ts` (skipping test files), writes html, clear-text and progress reports, and sets `coverageAnalysis: "perTest"`, so each mutant only runs the tests that cover it. `ignorePatterns` stops Stryker from copying the mock budget files into its sandbox. |
| `packages/loot-core/vitest.stryker.config.ts` | Extends the normal `vitest.config.ts` but limits `include` to `src/server/budget/**/*.test.ts`. The comment explains why: Stryker forces Vitest's `threads` pool, and on Windows the full loot-core suite crashes there because of native SQLite. Even on macOS this keeps the first test run much shorter.                        |
| `packages/loot-core/package.json`             | Adds the `mutation-test` script (`stryker run`) and devDeps `@stryker-mutator/core` and `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` (^10.0.0).                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `.gitignore`                                  | Ignores `.stryker-tmp` (the sandbox) and `reports/mutation/`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `ai-logs/sprint2/.../install-striker.md`      | Bennett's AI log of the `stryker init` session, which records why each init answer was chosen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

A few things to know before approving:

- **CI tells you nothing.** Every check was cancelled or skipped, and there are no reviews yet. You'd have to run it locally to know it works.
- **The setup is sound.** `mergeConfig` keeps the base setup file (`src/mocks/setup.ts`), the excludes and the peggy plugin, so the budget tests run in the same environment as `yarn test`.
- **The scope is narrow on purpose.** Only budget code gets mutated. Testing other areas means changing both `mutate` in the Stryker config and `include` in the Vitest config.
- **No release note.** Upstream's `check-release-notes` would flag that. It probably doesn't matter for this fork, since this is a dev-only tool.

## Setting it up locally

Your working tree is clean, so it's safe to switch branches. Run everything from the repo root:

```bash
# 1. Get the branch
gh pr checkout 91

# 2. Install the new Stryker packages (Node >= 22)
yarn install

# 3. Quick check: one source file only
yarn workspace @actual-app/core run mutation-test --mutate "src/server/budget/sort-categories.ts"

# 4. Full run over everything in src/server/budget
yarn workspace @actual-app/core run mutation-test

# 5. Open the HTML report
open packages/loot-core/reports/mutation/mutation.html
```

Tips:

- **Start with step 3.** A full run makes thousands of mutants across files like `goal-template.ts`, so it can take a long time. Stryker starts with a clean run of the budget tests; if any of them fail, it stops right away.
- **Reading the report:** survived mutants are the weak spots. The code changed and no test caught it. Killed mutants mean a test failed on the change, which is what you want. The mutation score shown at the end is killed ÷ (killed + survived) and doesn't count mutants with no test coverage.
- **When finished,** `git checkout docs/sprint1-report` takes you back. `.stryker-tmp/` and `reports/` are gitignored, so you won't leave stray files behind.

I can check out the branch and do the install and the one-file run for you if you'd like.

## Step 1: Create a branch and check your tools

**Why:** Starting from an up-to-date `master` means you're building on the same code everyone else has. A separate branch keeps your experiments out of your Sprint 1 report branch. Checking Node and Yarn versions first catches the most common setup failure before it turns into a confusing install error later.

**Run these from the repo root:**

```bash
# Check your tools
node -v     # needs v22 or higher
yarn -v     # needs 4.x

# Start from an up-to-date master and create the branch
git switch master
git pull
git switch -c chore/stryker-setup
```

**What you should see:**

- `node -v` prints something like `v22.x.x`. If it's lower, run `nvm use`, because the repo has an `.nvmrc` that picks the right version.
- `yarn -v` prints `4.x.x`. If it shows `1.x`, run `corepack enable`. This repo sets its Yarn version in `package.json`, and Corepack is what makes the `yarn` command use that version.
- The last command prints `Switched to a new branch 'chore/stryker-setup'`.

**Tip for your friend:** If `git switch master` complains about uncommitted changes, they should commit or stash them first. Your tree is already clean, so you won't hit this.

Run those and paste the output (or tell me it went fine), and we'll move on to Step 2: installing the packages.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 18:49:24-0400)**_

## `git switch` vs `git checkout`

For changing branches they do the same thing. `git switch -c foo` is the same as `git checkout -b foo`.

The difference is that `checkout` does two unrelated jobs:

- **switching branches:** `git checkout master`
- **overwriting files:** `git checkout -- file.ts` throws away your uncommitted edits to that file

Because one command does both, a typo or a file named like a branch can wipe out work you meant to keep. Git 2.23 (2019) split `checkout` into two safer commands: `git switch` for branches and `git restore` for files. `switch` only ever changes branches, so it can't discard edits by accident. If your friend's Git is older than 2.23, `checkout -b` works the same way.

---

## Step 2: Install the Stryker packages into loot-core

**What you're installing:**

- **`@stryker-mutator/core`** is the engine and the `stryker` command. It copies the project into a sandbox, creates _mutants_ (small deliberate bugs, like changing `>` to `>=` or `+` to `-`), runs your tests against each one, and writes the reports.
- **`@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner`** is a plugin that lets Stryker run tests with **Vitest**, which is what this repo uses. It also tracks which tests cover which lines, so each mutant only runs the tests that matter.

**Why loot-core, and why a dev dependency:** This repo is a Yarn monorepo with many packages. Stryker goes in `packages/loot-core` because that's where the budget logic and its tests live. It's a dev dependency (`-D`) because it's a testing tool and never ships to users.

**Why not `npx stryker init`:** Init runs its own install commands, which can be unreliable in a Yarn 4 monorepo and may put packages in the wrong `package.json`. Installing by hand also shows you what each piece does, which helps when you explain it to someone else.

**Run from the repo root:**

```bash
yarn workspace @actual-app/core add -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner
```

`yarn workspace @actual-app/core` means "run this inside the loot-core package," so you never `cd` into it. That's the rule in this repo's AGENTS.md: always run yarn from the root. `@actual-app/core` is loot-core's package name.

**Check that it worked:**

```bash
git diff --stat
yarn workspace @actual-app/core run stryker --version
```

**What you should see:**

- `git diff --stat` shows `packages/loot-core/package.json` with about 2 added lines and `yarn.lock` with roughly a thousand. Stryker brings in a lot of dependencies.
- The second command prints a version number, probably `10.x`. That means the `stryker` command is installed and runs from loot-core.

**If something goes wrong:**

- **Peer dependency warnings** (codes like `YN0060` or `YN0002`) are usually fine. They're warnings, not errors.
- **The two Stryker packages must be the same major version.** Installing them together in one command makes sure of that. If a friend adds them one at a time later, the versions can drift apart, and Stryker will refuse to load the plugin.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 18:58:28-0400)**_

## Is `/core` part of Stryker's name?

Yes, it's Stryker's own name. It has nothing to do with `@actual-app/core`, and the matching `/core` is a coincidence.

npm package names can have two parts: **`@scope/package`**.

- The **scope** (`@stryker-mutator`) is like an organization. It groups every package that team publishes.
- The **package** (`core`) is one specific package within that group.

The Stryker team publishes several packages under their scope, and `core` is the main engine. "Core" is a common name for "the main package" in projects split into pieces. Actual Budget made the same choice for `@actual-app/core`, which sits alongside its other `@actual-app/*` packages.

There's no package called just `stryker-mutator`. Very old versions of Stryker were published as plain `stryker`, but those are deprecated, so tell your friend to ignore old tutorials that say `npm install stryker`.

## Yes, the vitest-runner is there because we use Vitest

Stryker is built from plugins. The core knows how to create mutants, but not how to run any particular test framework. Each framework has its own runner plugin:

| Your tests use…        | Install                          |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **Vitest** (this repo) | `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` |
| Jest                   | `@stryker-mutator/jest-runner`   |
| Mocha                  | `@stryker-mutator/mocha-runner`  |
| Karma, Jasmine, …      | their own `-runner` packages     |

This way someone using Jest doesn't download Vitest support, and the reverse.

**Why not just use the core?** Stryker has a built-in fallback called the `command` runner, which just runs `npm test` for every mutant. It works with any framework, but it's much slower. It can't tell which tests cover which lines, so every mutant reruns the whole suite. The vitest-runner can track that per test, so each mutant only runs the few tests that touch its code. We'll turn this on in Step 3 with `coverageAnalysis: "perTest"`.

**A rule your friend can use:** install `core`, plus one runner that matches the project's test framework. To find the framework, look for a `vitest.config.*` or `jest.config.*` file, or check the `test` script in `package.json`.

Once the install finishes and `stryker --version` prints a version, tell me and we'll write `stryker.config.json` in Step 3.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 19:00:23-0400)**_

Yes, the wizard is a fine way to do it. The one thing to avoid is `npm install`.

## Why not `npm install`

This repo uses Yarn 4, and npm doesn't understand some of its setup. For example, loot-core's `package.json` has dependencies like `"@actual-app/crdt": "workspace:*"`, a Yarn-only syntax. `npm install` tends to fail on these, and even when it gets further, it creates a `package-lock.json` that conflicts with `yarn.lock` and can leave `node_modules` broken. Your friend should never run `npm install` in this repo.

## The wizard: `npm init stryker`

Stryker's official setup command is:

```bash
cd packages/loot-core
npm init stryker@latest
```

Despite the `npm`, this doesn't install anything with npm. `npm init stryker` downloads and runs Stryker's setup wizard, which asks a few questions, writes a config file, and installs the packages **with whichever package manager you choose**. Bennett used this path in PR 91. His AI log has the answers:

| Prompt           | Answer                                                     |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Framework?       | **None/other** (this repo uses Vite, not create-react-app) |
| Test runner?     | **vitest**, which installs the `vitest-runner` for you     |
| Build command?   | **leave empty** (Vitest compiles TypeScript on the fly)    |
| Reporters?       | **html, clear-text, progress** (the defaults)              |
| Package manager? | **yarn** ← the important one                               |
| Config format?   | **JSON**                                                   |

You have to `cd` into `packages/loot-core` first. The wizard installs into whatever folder you're in, and if you run it from the repo root, the packages land in the root `package.json`.

## Which should you use?

- **Wizard:** easier to explain to a friend, since it's one command and a few questions. It writes the starter config for you.
- **Manual `yarn workspace … add`:** the same result as one command. It looked complicated here because I explained each piece, not because it has more steps.

Either way, you'll make the same edits to the generated config afterward: which files to mutate, and which Vitest config to use. That's Step 3.

**Where you are now:**

- **If you already ran the `yarn workspace … add` command,** Step 2 is done and you don't need the wizard. We'll write the config by hand in Step 3.
- **If you haven't,** run the wizard instead, then paste me the `stryker.config.json` it creates and we'll adjust it together.

Which path did you take?

_**User (2026-10-11 19:05:41-0400)**_

for “Which reporter(s) do you want to use?” why do we use the default, why html, clear-text, and progress, and not dashboard? What does each of these mean?

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 19:06:01-0400)**_

A **reporter** decides where Stryker sends its results. You can pick several, and they all run during the same mutation run. The three defaults cover three different moments: **while it runs**, **right after**, and **when you dig in**.

## progress: while it's running

This shows a live progress bar in the terminal:

```
Mutation testing  [====------] 42% | 312/740 | 🎉 280 🙁 25 ⏰ 7 | ~3m remaining
```

That line shows how many mutants have been tested, how many were killed or survived, and an estimated time left. Mutation runs can take many minutes, and without this the terminal sits silent and you can't tell whether Stryker is working or stuck.

## clear-text: right after it finishes

This prints the results in the terminal when the run ends, in two parts:

1. **Every survived mutant**, with its file, line, and the exact change. For example:
   ```
   [Survived] EqualityOperator
   src/server/budget/goal-template.ts:142:9
   -   if (amount > 0) {
   +   if (amount >= 0) {
   ```
   This means that when Stryker changed `>` to `>=`, every test still passed, so no test checks what happens when `amount` is exactly 0.
2. **A summary table** with each file's mutation score and counts of killed, survived, timed-out, and uncovered mutants.

It's good for a quick check without leaving the terminal. On a big run, the list of survivors can get long.

## html: when you dig in

This writes an interactive web page to `packages/loot-core/reports/mutation/mutation.html`. You open the file directly in a browser, no server needed. It shows:

- a folder tree with a score for each file, so you can spot weak files quickly
- your source code with each mutant marked inline: green for killed, red for survived
- what each mutant changed, and which tests ran against it

This is the reporter you'll use most. It's the easiest way to find gaps in your tests and decide which tests to write next.

## dashboard: why we skip it

This one **uploads your results to Stryker's public website** (dashboard.stryker-mutator.io). Projects use it to track their mutation score over time and to show a score badge in their README. We skip it because:

- **It takes setup:** you sign in with GitHub, enable the repo on the dashboard, and provide an API key through an environment variable. Without the key it just fails.
- **It's built for CI:** it's useful when every push uploads automatically, not for runs on your own laptop.
- **It publishes your results:** they go to a public website, which a class project doesn't need.

## Can you change your mind later?

Yes. The answer just becomes a line in `stryker.config.json`:

```json
"reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress"]
```

Edit the list whenever you like. One extra worth knowing about: adding `"json"` also writes `mutation.json`, which helps if you ever want to process the results with a script.

**One sentence for your friend:** progress tells you it's working, clear-text gives you a quick summary, html lets you investigate, and dashboard is for publishing results online, which we don't need.

When the wizard finishes, paste me the `stryker.config.json` it created and we'll adjust it in Step 3.

_**User (2026-10-11 19:08:32-0400)**_

why do we want our config file to be json and not javascript?

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 19:08:45-0400)**_

Our settings are fixed values like which files to mutate and which reporters to use, and JSON is the simplest format for fixed values. You'd only need JavaScript if a setting had to be calculated when Stryker starts.

## Why JSON fits here

- **It's easy to read.** It's just keys and values, so your friend can read it without knowing any JavaScript.
- **VS Code autocomplete.** The wizard adds a `"$schema"` line at the top that points to Stryker's list of valid settings. VS Code uses it to suggest settings as you type, show what each one means on hover, and underline typos (like `"mutat"` instead of `"mutate"`) before you ever run Stryker.
- **It's just data.** A JSON file can't run code, so there's nothing in it to debug.
- **Clean diffs.** In a PR, a change shows up as one line, like `"mutate": [...]`, which makes it easy for reviewers to see what changed.

## When JavaScript would be better

The JavaScript option is `stryker.config.mjs`, a file that exports the settings. Because it's code, you can calculate values when Stryker starts:

```js
export default {
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  // run fewer mutants on CI, more locally
  mutate: process.env.CI
    ? ['src/server/budget/goal-template.ts']
    : ['src/server/budget/**/*.ts'],
};
```

Use it when you need environment variables, conditions, or values read from other files. You'd also want it if you wanted real comments.

## The JSON quirks to warn your friend about

1. **No comments.** JSON doesn't allow `//` comments. That's why the wizard's file has keys like `"_comment": "..."` and `"testRunner_comment": "..."`. Stryker ignores those keys, so they act as comments.
2. **No trailing commas.** `["html", "progress",]` is invalid JSON, and Stryker won't load the file. This is the most common mistake when people edit JSON by hand. The `$schema` underlining in VS Code catches it.

**One sentence for your friend:** use JSON when the settings are fixed values, and JavaScript only when a setting needs to be calculated.

Once the wizard is done, paste me the `stryker.config.json` it created, and we'll start Step 3 and adjust it for this repo.

## What the wizard did

You picked the right answers. The config has yarn, vitest, the three reporters and JSON, and no `package-lock.json` was created. It also added `.stryker-tmp` to `.gitignore`, which is the folder where Stryker keeps its sandbox copy of the code. Keep that change.

There's one problem: it ran from the **repo root**, so everything went to the wrong place.

|                                       | Where it went       | Where it belongs                  |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| The two `@stryker-mutator/*` packages | root `package.json` | `packages/loot-core/package.json` |
| `stryker.config.json`                 | repo root           | `packages/loot-core/`             |

**Why it matters:** Stryker treats the folder its config is in as the project. At the root, it would try to mutate and test the whole monorepo and couldn't find loot-core's Vitest setup. The packages also belong with the code they test, so anyone reading loot-core's `package.json` can see it uses Stryker.

This mistake is easy to make, so it's worth warning your friend about. The fix follows.

---

## Step 2b: Move Stryker into loot-core

Run from the repo root:

```bash
# 1. Remove the packages from the root package.json
yarn remove @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

# 2. Add them to loot-core instead
yarn workspace @actual-app/core add -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

# 3. Move the config file into loot-core
mv stryker.config.json packages/loot-core/
```

Use plain `mv` here, not `git mv`. The file isn't tracked by git yet, so there's nothing for git to move.

**4. Fix the `$schema` path.** Open `packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json` and change the first setting:

```json
"$schema": "../../node_modules/@stryker-mutator/core/schema/stryker-schema.json",
```

The old path `./node_modules/...` worked at the root. Now that the file is two folders deeper, it has to go back up to the root's `node_modules` with `../../`. Yarn installs shared packages there even when they belong to a workspace. If the path is wrong, nothing breaks, but VS Code stops autocompleting and checking your settings.

**Check that it worked:**

```bash
git status --short
yarn workspace @actual-app/core run stryker --version
```

You should see:

- `M packages/loot-core/package.json` and `?? packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json`
- **no** `M package.json` (the root). If it's still listed, step 1 didn't work.
- `M .gitignore` and `M yarn.lock` (both expected)
- a version number, around `10.x`

Tell me when that looks right and we'll start Step 3: telling Stryker which files to mutate and which Vitest config to use.

## Step 3: Write `stryker.config.json`

**Why:** The config file tells Stryker three things: which test framework to use, which source files to put bugs (mutants) into, and how to report the results. Stryker looks for this file in the folder you run it from. Our script in Step 5 will run it from `packages/loot-core`, so that's where the file goes.

**Create `packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json` with:**

```json
{
  "$schema": "../../node_modules/@stryker-mutator/core/schema/stryker-schema.json",
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "vitest": {
    "configFile": "vitest.stryker.config.ts"
  },
  "mutate": ["src/server/budget/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts"],
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest",
  "reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress"]
}
```

### What each line does

**`$schema`** points VS Code to Stryker's list of valid settings, so you get autocomplete and typo warnings. It's `../../` because Yarn installs the package in the repo root's `node_modules`, two folders up. Stryker ignores this line; only the editor uses it.

**`testRunner: "vitest"`** tells Stryker to use the vitest-runner plugin you installed in Step 2.

**`vitest.configFile`** names the Vitest config Stryker should use. loot-core has two Vitest configs (`vitest.config.ts` for Node and `vitest.web.config.ts` for the browser build), so we have to pick one. We point to **`vitest.stryker.config.ts`, which doesn't exist yet.** We'll create it in Step 4, and that step explains why we need a third config. Until then Stryker won't run, which is expected.

**`mutate`** lists the files Stryker puts bugs into. It's the most important setting:

- `src/server/budget/**/*.ts` means every `.ts` file under `src/server/budget`, including subfolders (that's the `**`). This is the budget logic, like `goal-template.ts`, `actions.ts` and `sort-categories.ts`.
- `!src/**/*.test.ts` excludes test files. The `!` means "except". Mutating your tests makes no sense: you want to check whether the tests catch bugs in the code, not put bugs in the tests.
- The `.pegjs` grammar files in that folder are skipped automatically, because they don't end in `.ts`. Stryker can't mutate them anyway.

We start with one folder because every mutant means running tests again. Mutating all of loot-core would create tens of thousands of mutants and take hours. Your friend can point `mutate` at whatever area they're responsible for.

**`coverageAnalysis: "perTest"`** makes Stryker first record which tests run which lines. Then, for each mutant, it runs only the tests that touch that line. There are three options:

- `"off"`: run every test for every mutant. Correct, but very slow.
- `"all"`: skip mutants that no test touches at all.
- `"perTest"`: skip those, and also run only the relevant tests. This is the fastest, and the vitest-runner supports it.

**`reporters`** are the three we covered earlier: progress while it runs, clear-text when it finishes, html for digging in.

**What we left out of the wizard's version:**

- `_comment` and `testRunner_comment` were just notes, so we don't need them.
- `packageManager` only matters to the wizard itself.

### Check that it worked

Open the file in VS Code:

- **There should be no red or yellow underlines.** If there are, the `$schema` path is probably wrong, or there's a trailing comma.
- Hover over `"coverageAnalysis"`. A description from Stryker's schema should pop up, which tells you `$schema` is working.

**Don't run Stryker yet.** It will fail because `vitest.stryker.config.ts` doesn't exist. That's Step 4.

I'm reading "this" as creating the config file. If you meant something else, like the `$schema` hover, let me know.

## Why the config isn't created for you

Installing a package only downloads its code into `node_modules`. Package managers never create config files, because only you know the answers:

- **Which files should be mutated?** Stryker can't guess in a monorepo. Mutating everything would take hours.
- **Which Vitest config should it use?** loot-core has two, and we're about to add a third.

Stryker does have a fallback. If there's no config file, it uses defaults: it mutates everything under `src/` and tests with the `command` runner, which just runs `npm test`. In this repo that would mean all of loot-core's code, run against both test suites, with no per-test coverage. That's very slow, and `npm test` in a Yarn repo can go wrong.

The `npm init stryker` wizard is the automatic version, but even it can't answer those two questions. That's why Bennett still had to add `mutate` and `vitest` by hand afterward.

## Creating the file from the command line

Run this from the repo root:

```bash
cat > packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "../../node_modules/@stryker-mutator/core/schema/stryker-schema.json",
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "vitest": {
    "configFile": "vitest.stryker.config.ts"
  },
  "mutate": ["src/server/budget/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts"],
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest",
  "reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress"]
}
EOF
```

**How it works:**

- `cat > file` writes whatever comes after it into `file`, creating the file or **overwriting it if it exists**.
- `<<'EOF'` … `EOF` is a _heredoc_. Everything between the two `EOF` lines becomes the input to `cat`.
- **The quotes around `'EOF'` matter.** Without them, the shell treats `$schema` as a variable. Since it's not set, it becomes an empty string, and your file silently ends up with `"": "../../node_modules/..."`. The quotes tell the shell to copy the text exactly as written. This is a good gotcha to warn your friend about.

**Check that it's valid JSON from the command line:**

```bash
node -e "JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync('packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json','utf8')); console.log('valid JSON')"
```

This prints `valid JSON` or an error pointing at the problem, like a trailing comma. Node is already installed for this repo, so it works on any machine.

You could also run the wizard again the right way, with `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run stryker init`. `yarn workspace` runs it inside loot-core, so the file would land in the right place. But you'd still have to edit it afterward, so the heredoc is quicker.

Once `valid JSON` prints, tell me and we'll do Step 4: the Stryker-specific Vitest config.

how do we run the command without doing cd? would it be npm init packages/loot-core stryker@latest?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 19:38:51-0400)**_

No, that won't work. `npm init` takes exactly one thing to run, called the _initializer_. In your command, `packages/loot-core` would be read as the initializer. npm reads a name with a slash in it as a GitHub repo, so it would go looking for something to download at that address. The `stryker@latest` part would be passed along as an extra argument.

## Use a subshell

```bash
(cd packages/loot-core && npm init stryker@latest)
```

- **The parentheses** run everything inside them in a _subshell_, a temporary child copy of your terminal.
- **`cd packages/loot-core`** changes folders only inside that subshell.
- **`&&`** means "run the next command only if the previous one worked." So if you mistype the path, the `cd` fails and the wizard **doesn't** run in the wrong folder. That's the mistake you hit earlier, so this protects against it.
- When the wizard finishes, the subshell exits and your terminal is **still at the repo root**. There's no `cd ../..` to forget.

It still uses `cd`, but your terminal never actually leaves the root, which is the point.

## Why not an npm flag?

npm has flags like `--prefix` and `-w` (workspace) that look like they should do this, but they don't fit:

- **`-w`** is for npm workspaces. With `init`, it's meant to **create** a new workspace, and npm might try to edit the root `package.json` and run its own install. That's what we're avoiding.
- **`--prefix`** changes where npm installs packages, not necessarily the folder the wizard writes its config in.

Yarn has a clean no-`cd` form, `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run stryker init`, but it only works once Stryker is already installed. The subshell is the simplest option that works from a clean start.

```text
## StrykerJS Monorepo Overview

StrykerJS operates as a monorepo where all official stryker packages are maintained, and packages are located in the packages folder.

## General Monorepo Workspace Configuration

While the search results don't contain specific details about per-package configuration in StrykerJS, they do provide general information about how monorepos with workspaces are structured:

You configure workspaces by adding folders to the workspaces field in your root package.json file, which contains a list of workspace folders in the form of globs.

To enable workspaces, you add the workspaces key to your root-level package.json, which should list all directories containing the workspaces.

Each workspace has a unique name, which is specified in its package.json.
```

Stryker has no monorepo mode. You set it up separately in each package you want to mutation-test, which is what we're doing. The `$schema` path is the only part that doesn't account for a monorepo, and there are a few ways around it.

## Stryker isn't monorepo-aware

I couldn't find a workspace or monorepo option anywhere in Stryker's docs. Each package gets its own config file and runs separately, and Stryker treats the folder you run it from as a standalone project. That's why the wizard had to run inside `packages/loot-core`.

The `./node_modules/...` path is copied straight from [Stryker's config-file docs](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/config-file/), which assume one package with its own `node_modules`. In a Yarn monorepo, packages are installed once at the root, so the path doesn't match. Stryker itself doesn't care; only VS Code uses `$schema`.

The other two edits aren't about the monorepo. **`mutate`** and **`vitest.configFile`** are needed because loot-core is large and has multiple Vitest configs. A single-package project of that size would need them too.

## Your options for `$schema`

| Option                                                             | How                                                                                                                   | Trade-off                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **1. Keep `../../`** (recommended)                                 | What you have now                                                                                                     | Matches the Stryker version you installed. Same as PR 91.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **2. Rename the file to `stryker.conf.json` and delete `$schema`** | VS Code finds the schema by itself                                                                                    | [SchemaStore](https://www.schemastore.org/api/json/catalog.json), the catalog VS Code uses to find schemas, recognizes `stryker.conf.json` but **not** `stryker.config.json`. Its schema comes from Stryker's latest code on GitHub, so it may not match your installed version. It also wouldn't match PR 91's file name. |
| **3. Use the web URL**                                             | `"$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stryker-mutator/stryker/master/packages/api/schema/stryker-core.json"` | Works from any folder depth, but has the same version mismatch as option 2.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **4. Delete `$schema`**                                            | Remove the line                                                                                                       | Stryker runs the same. You only lose autocomplete and typo warnings.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

I checked that the URL in options 2 and 3 still works.

**My recommendation:** keep `../../`. It's one line, it matches the version you installed, and the reason is easy to explain: Yarn installs packages at the root, so the path goes up two folders. If your friend ever moves the config deeper, they just add more `../`.

Will bail on the first test failure (unless you set disableBail to true ). This is done to boost performance. Will disable code coverage reporting This is done because StrykerJS uses it's own coverage analysis , which is supported. Will report the location of each test This is done so incremental mode can tell which tests changed. In-source testing ​ Vitest's in-source testing is supported. Short answer: Stryker changes how Vitest runs, and loot-core's full test suite doesn't cope well with those changes. A separate config lets Stryker run only the tests it needs, without changing how `yarn test` works for everyone else.

## What Stryker changes about Vitest

According to the [vitest-runner docs](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/vitest-runner/), Stryker forces these settings, and **you can't override them**:

| Stryker forces                     | What it means for loot-core                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **`threads: true`**                | Tests run in worker threads instead of Vitest's usual separate processes. loot-core's tests use **native SQLite** (`better-sqlite3`), and native modules can crash in worker threads. That's the Windows crash Bennett hit in PR 91. |
| **`bail: 1`**                      | Stops at the **first** failing test.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| An initial test run that must pass | Before creating any mutants, Stryker runs your tests once without changes. If anything fails, it stops.                                                                                                                              |

Taken together: if Stryker loads the full loot-core suite, **any** test anywhere in loot-core that crashes in threads mode, or fails for unrelated reasons, stops your mutation run, even though you're only mutating budget code.

## What the new config does

```ts
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'vitest/config';

import baseConfig from './vitest.config';

export default mergeConfig(
  baseConfig,
  defineConfig({
    test: {
      include: ['src/server/budget/**/*.test.ts'],
    },
  }),
);
```

- **`mergeConfig(baseConfig, …)`** reuses everything from the normal `vitest.config.ts`: the setup file, the peggy plugin and the excludes. Budget tests run in the same environment as always, and if someone changes the base config, Stryker's config picks up the change.
- **`include`** is the only override. It loads just the budget tests, which match the files in `mutate`.

**Why a new file instead of editing `vitest.config.ts`?** Changing `include` there would stop `yarn test` from running every other loot-core test, for everyone on the team.

## A simpler alternative I found

While checking the docs, I found that the vitest-runner has a **`dir`** option that limits where Vitest looks for test files. It could do the same thing without a new file:

```json
"vitest": {
  "configFile": "vitest.config.ts",
  "dir": "src/server/budget"
}
```

I haven't tested this here. Since the PR adds its own config file, I'd stick with that for consistency with your team, and mention `dir` as an option.

## A correction

Earlier I said `coverageAnalysis: "perTest"` is what turns on per-test coverage. According to the same docs, **the vitest-runner ignores that setting and always uses perTest.** The line in your config does nothing. It's harmless, so keep it or delete it. Sorry for getting that wrong.

**One line for your friend:** Stryker forces Vitest into a mode that loot-core's full test suite doesn't handle well, so we give Stryker its own config that runs only the budget tests.

Ready for Step 4? Creating this file is the step.

Sources:

- [Stryker Mutator: Vitest runner](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/vitest-runner/)

## Step 3: Edit `stryker.config.json`

Replace the contents of `packages/loot-core/stryker.config.json` with:

```json
{
  "$schema": "../../node_modules/@stryker-mutator/core/schema/stryker-schema.json",
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "vitest": {
    "configFile": "vitest.config.ts",
    "dir": "src/server/budget"
  },
  "mutate": ["src/server/budget/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts"],
  "reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress"]
}
```

**What's different from the version I gave you before:**

- **`vitest.configFile` is now the normal `vitest.config.ts`.** loot-core has two Vitest configs, so naming one avoids guessing. The budget tests get the same setup they always use.
- **`vitest.dir` is new.** It tells Vitest to look for test files only in `src/server/budget`. The initial test run and every mutant then use just those 9 budget test files. A crash or failure elsewhere in loot-core can't stop your run.
- **`coverageAnalysis` is gone,** because the vitest-runner ignores it and always uses perTest.

**One thing to warn your friend about:** `mutate` and `dir` must point at the **same area**. If they change `mutate` to, say, `src/server/accounts/**/*.ts`, they also need to change `dir` to `src/server/accounts`. Otherwise Stryker mutates code that none of the loaded tests cover, and every mutant shows up as "no coverage."

**Check that it worked** (from the repo root):


Then hover over `"testRunner"` in VS Code to confirm the `$schema` path works.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-11 19:57:37-0400)**_

`dir` tells Vitest **which folder to search for test files**.

## How Vitest finds tests

Normally Vitest starts at the project folder (`packages/loot-core`), searches every subfolder, and collects every file whose name matches its test pattern, like `*.test.ts`. In loot-core that's every test file in the package: accounts, budget, rules, sync and so on.

`dir` changes the starting point of that search:

```
packages/loot-core/          ← default: search starts here (all of loot-core)
└── src/
    └── server/
        ├── accounts/        ✗ not searched
        ├── rules/           ✗ not searched
        └── budget/          ← with "dir": "src/server/budget", search starts here
            ├── actions.test.ts         ✓
            ├── goal-template.test.ts   ✓
            └── ... (9 test files)      ✓
```

This is what I checked a moment ago: with `--dir src/server/budget`, Vitest listed exactly the 9 budget test files and nothing else.

## What it doesn't change

`dir` only changes **where Vitest looks for tests**. Everything else still comes from `vitest.config.ts`, as usual: the setup file (`src/mocks/setup.ts`), the plugins, the excludes. The budget tests run exactly as they do with `yarn test`. There are just fewer of them.

## Why we want it for Stryker

Before making any mutants, Stryker runs all the tests Vitest found, once, and **every one has to pass**. Without `dir`, that means all of loot-core's tests, run in the threads mode Stryker forces. Any crash or failure anywhere stops your run, even in code you're not mutating. With `dir`, only the budget tests have to pass, and those are the only tests that matter for budget mutants anyway.

## Where it comes from

It's a regular Vitest option (`vitest --dir <path>` on the command line). Stryker's `"vitest": { "dir": ... }` setting just passes it through to Vitest.

**One line for your friend:** `dir` is the folder Vitest searches for tests, so we point it at the same folder we're mutating.

When your config is updated and shows `valid JSON`, we'll do Step 4: the `mutation-test` script.

When Stryker mutates something in `budget/base.ts` or `budget/actions.ts`, these three tests might have caught it, but with `dir` they never run. That mutant is then reported as **survived** even though some test in the repo would catch it.

At least two of the three seem to use budget code as **setup**: `createBudget` and `createAllBudgets` build a budget so the test can check something else. A test that only uses a function as setup usually won't fail when that function has a small bug, so the real gap is probably smaller than it looks. I haven't verified this.

1. **Keep `dir`** (recommended for now). It's fast and reliable, and it gets your first run working. When you read the report, take survivors in `base.ts` and `actions.ts` with a grain of salt.
2. **Remove `dir`** so all 71 test files are available. Each mutant still runs only the relevant tests: the vitest-runner's `related` option is on by default and picks the tests that import the mutated file. The catch is that the **initial run** runs all 71 in threads mode, and that's where the SQLite crash or an unrelated failing test could stop you. Bennett hit the crash on Windows. You're on a Mac, so it might work. That's worth an experiment once the basic setup works.
3. **Add just those three files.** `dir` only takes one folder, so this would need the separate Vitest config file after all, with `include` listing the budget folder plus the three files.

## Step 4: Add a `mutation-test` script and ignore the reports

### Part A: The script

**Why:** Without a script, you'd type `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run stryker run`, which is easy to get wrong. With a script, there's a short, memorable name, and anyone who opens loot-core's `package.json` can see that mutation testing exists.

In `packages/loot-core/package.json`, find the `scripts` section. Add one line after `test:web`:

```json
    "test:web": "ENV=web vitest --run -c vitest.web.config.ts",
    "mutation-test": "stryker run",
```

**The name matters.** Look at loot-core's `test` script, two lines above:

```json
"test": "npm-run-all -cp 'test:*'",
```

`test:*` means "run every script whose name starts with `test:`." If you named yours **`test:mutation`**, then every `yarn test`, run by every teammate and by CI, would also start a full Stryker run, which takes minutes and has nothing to do with normal testing. `mutation-test` doesn't start with `test:`, so it stays separate. That's an important warning for your friend.

### Part B: Ignore the reports

**Why:** Every run writes the HTML report to `packages/loot-core/reports/mutation/`. That folder is generated output, like a build, so it shouldn't be committed. The wizard already ignored `.stryker-tmp`, the sandbox folder, but not the reports.

Add two lines to the end of `packages/loot-core/.gitignore`:

```
# stryker reports
reports/mutation
```

It goes in loot-core's `.gitignore`, next to the wizard's entry, because that's the folder Stryker runs from. A `.gitignore` applies to its own folder and everything inside it.

### Check that it worked

From the repo root:

```bash
# Is the script wired up? Prints Stryker's help for "run", without starting a run
yarn workspace @actual-app/core run mutation-test --help

# Would the report be ignored? (works even before the file exists)
git check-ignore -v packages/loot-core/reports/mutation/mutation.html
```

**What you should see:**

- The first command prints usage text that starts with something like `Usage: stryker run [options]`. If it says `Couldn't find a script named "mutation-test"`, check the spelling and the comma at the end of the line before it.
- The second prints the `.gitignore` line that matched, like `packages/loot-core/.gitignore:7:reports/mutation`. If it prints **nothing**, the file isn't ignored. Check the spelling.

Also, `git status --short` should now show `M packages/loot-core/package.json` and `M packages/loot-core/.gitignore` among the changes. That's expected.

Tell me what both commands print, and then Step 5 is the first real run, on a single file.

> If you're on **Windows** and Stryker's initial test run crashes, add `"dir": "src/server/budget"` inside the `"vitest"` block. That limits the tests to the budget folder, so the full suite doesn't crash.

## Why the path says "server"

Here, `server` doesn't mean a web server. loot-core keeps its core logic, the part that does the budget calculations and talks to the database, in `src/server/`. Budget logic is in `src/server/budget/`, so that's where we point `mutate`.

Once the `.gitignore` line from Step 4 is in and `git check-ignore` prints a match, we'll do Step 5: the first real run on `sort-categories.ts`.

# Committing Changes in actualbudget/actual

Before creating any git commit or pull request in this repo, read:

**`.github/agents/pr-and-commit-rules.md`**

It is the authoritative source for the rules you must apply yourself: the `[AI]` PR-title prefix and leaving the PR template blank (and the Chinese exception). The mechanical commit/git rules are enforced by tooling and aren't restated there. Read it on every commit/PR session so any updates are picked up automatically.

## The one rule worth restating

Every commit message and every pull request title MUST begin with `[AI]`. Commit messages are checked by the git-guard hook (a missing prefix is blocked before the commit lands), so the one that needs _your_ attention is the PR title — nothing checks it for you, and the cost of forgetting it is high since the PR has to be renamed by hand. Examples:

- `[AI] Fix type error in account validation` — correct
- `Fix type error in account validation` — wrong, missing prefix

The PR-template rule and the rest live in the rules file. Read it before each commit/PR rather than relying on this skill's summary, because the rules file evolves and this skill deliberately does not restate it.

## Why this matters

Maintainers triage AI-authored contributions separately, and the `[AI]` prefix is what makes that triage fast — it also drives the automatic `"AI generated"` PR label, so getting the prefix right is the one action that gates the whole triage path. Without it the PR looks like a normal human contribution and the wrong review process gets applied. The "do not fill in the PR template" rule exists because the human is the one who actually tested the change and can write the Description / Testing / Checklist sections honestly — an AI-filled template misrepresents who did what.

The rules file is short. Read it.
